query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing a moderate negative lattice misfit (around –0.14%) at the FCC/BCC interfaces in HEA multilayers stabilizes interfacial microstructure by enhancing phase integrity, thereby impeding dislocation climb and reducing creep rates under sustained loading.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA multilayers fabricated by sputtering with FCC and BCC layers that currently show random interfacial compositions and variable lattice misfit.
generation.intervention: Tailor the deposition process by adjusting target composition and deposition rates to achieve a controlled, moderate negative misfit near –0.14% at the interfaces.
generation.conditions: Sustained load experiments at intermediate-to-high temperatures where diffusion-assisted dislocation climb is active.
generation.structural_mediator: Stabilized interfaces with reduced atomic strain and preserved phase boundaries, confirmed via X-ray diffraction and high-resolution TEM.
generation.mechanism: A controlled moderate negative misfit reinforces the γ/γ′-like interfaces by lowering local strain and retarding dislocation climb, thus retarding the progression of creep deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Engineered multilayers will display a notable decrease in the steady-state creep rate, with a longer creep life and a reduction in accumulated atomic strain near the interfaces, compared to multilayers with randomly established misfit.
generation.baseline: Multilayers with uncontrolled interface misfits that exhibit higher atomic strain and faster creep due to enhanced dislocation climb.
generation.boundary: The misfit must lie within a moderate range; overly negative values may destabilize the interface, while too-small misfit would be ineffective.
generation.uncertainty: Although simulations (PMC12842692 series) suggest a moderate negative misfit enhances creep resistance, the precise optimal misfit may vary with composition and processing, necessitating further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of HEA multilayers: one with deposition parameters adjusted to achieve the targeted –0.14% lattice misfit at interfaces and one without misfit engineering. Conduct creep tests at the specified temperatures and perform in situ TEM to monitor dislocation climb and interfacial strain.
measurements: Determine lattice misfit using X-ray diffraction.
Measure steady-state creep rates and creep life.
Record dislocation dynamics and atomic strain fields near the interfaces via TEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered multilayers do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate or improvement in interface stability relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Effect of γ/γ′ Lattice Misfit on the Creep Properties of HESA
cited_evidence.text: As shown in Figure 13, all creep curves exhibit the typical three-stage behavior. Notably, the duration of the steady-state creep stage decreases with increasing |δ|. The relationship between creep life and |δ| is non-monotonic. Specifically, within the range of −0.1688% to −0.084%, creep life increases as |δ| increases. Conversely, within the range of −0.8075% to −0.1688%, creep life decreases as |δ| increases. The longest creep life is observed at δ = −0.1688%. To gain further insight into the underlying mechanisms, atomic strain distributions were analyzed, as shown in Figure 14. Figure 14a,b compare atomic strain maps of HESAs with negative (−0.1402%) and positive (0.1402%) lattice misfits. At t = 130 ps, the model with the negative lattice misfit (Figure 14a) exhibits lower atomic strain, suggesting enhanced resistance to deformation. This implies that a negative lattice misfit stabilizes the γ′ phase, strengthens the γ/γ′ interface, and impedes dislocation motion, thereby improving creep resistance. Figure 14c shows the atomic strain of HESA with δ = −0.1688% at 150 ps, further supporting the trend that moderate negative misfit enhances phase stability. This observation is co

In this paper, MD simulations are conducted to systematically investigate the creep behavior of HESAs under varying stress, temperature, γ/γ′ lattice misfit, and γ′ volume fraction. The creep mechanism and the critical creep resistance factors are explored. The main conclusions are summarized as follows: The creep behavior of both HESAs and HEAs is strongly influenced by stress and temperature, and their combined effect governs the rate of atomic rearrangement during deformation. As these parameters increase, the creep rate accelerates rapidly due to enhanced diffusion and easier activation of deformation carriers. Temperature plays a particularly dominant role, as high thermal energy significantly facilitates atomic mobility, vacancy migration, and interface-mediated processes. Compared with HEAs, HESAs consistently exhibit lower creep strain under identical conditions, and the difference becomes more pronounced at higher stress–temperature combinations, highlighting the intrinsic microstructural advantages of γ/γ′-strengthened systems.

papers.title: Small-Scale Insight into Uniform Deformability and Softening Resistance of Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: W-based refractory high-entropy alloys (e.g., WTaMoNbV HEA)
papers.approach: Nanoindentation, microcompression tests, TEM observations, and atomistic (MD) simulations to probe deformation response at different temperatures and orientations.
papers.findings: Increasing chemical complexity reduces elastic/plastic anisotropy, promotes extensive dislocation nucleation across multiple slip systems, and concurrently restricts long-range dislocation glide. The evolution from planar slip (with stress drops in elemental tungsten) to homogeneous smooth flow in HEAs was documented.
papers.mechanism: The severe lattice distortion elevates the Peierls barrier, thereby impeding extended dislocation glide while favoring cooperative edge and screw dislocation activity, which sustains strength and work hardening under varied temperatures.

papers.title: Creep Behavior and Its Influencing Factors in High-Entropy Superalloys: A Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study.
papers.system: High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) with γ/γ′ dual-phase structure and controlled lattice misfit
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics simulations that vary stress, temperature, and γ/γ′ lattice misfit. Detailed analysis of atomic strain distributions and creep curves.
papers.findings: Creep curves exhibit three-stage behavior. A moderate negative lattice misfit (e.g., around −0.1688%) optimizes phase stability and creep life, while excessive misfit deteriorates it. The simulations indicate that stress and temperature govern atomic rearrangements, with dislocation climb (assisted by lattice diffusion) playing a key role at lower stresses.
papers.mechanism: Improved creep resistance arises from a stabilized γ′ phase and a strengthened γ/γ′ interface that impedes dislocation motion. There is a transition in the dominant deformation mechanism as stress/temperature conditions vary.

papers.title: Intermediate-Temperature Creep Deformation and Microstructural Evolution of an Equiatomic FCC-Structured CoCrFeNiMn High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Tensile creep experiments over intermediate temperatures (500–600 °C) combined with optical microscopy and TEM to study dislocation substructure, dynamic recrystallization, and precipitation.
papers.findings: A stress-dependent transition from low-stress to high-stress creep regimes was observed, with low stress characterized by a stress exponent of 5–6 and high stress by exponents of 8.9–14. Dynamic recrystallization and precipitation were documented at higher stresses, which enhanced dislocation tangling and increased activation energy for creep deformation.
papers.mechanism: At lower stresses, stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion dominates, while at higher stresses, the cooperative effects of dynamic recrystallization and precipitate formation introduce additional barriers to dislocation motion.

papers.title: Nanoindentation into a bcc high-entropy HfNbTaTiZr alloy-an atomistic study of the effect of short-range order.
papers.system: BCC high-entropy alloy (HfNbTaTiZr, Senkov alloy) with and without short-range order (SRO)
papers.approach: Large-scale MD nanoindentation simulations comparing a random solid solution and one with mechanically introduced SRO via Monte Carlo procedures, with comparative studies to pure elemental Ta.
papers.findings: Introduction of SRO results in a slight stiffening of elastic constants and roughly a 10% increase in indentation hardness. Dislocation emission (nucleation) is impeded and dislocation recovery is constrained relative to pure Ta; the plastic zone remains larger with higher dislocation densities in the presence of SRO.
papers.mechanism: SRO (and associated local formation of HfTi-rich B2 precipitates) creates local barriers that elevate the force needed for dislocation nucleation and impede dislocation motion, leading to enhanced hardness and modified plastic deformation behavior.

papers.title: Nanoscale Indentation-Induced Crystal Plasticity in CrCoNi Medium-Entropy Alloys Containing Short-Range Order.
papers.system: CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy with short-range order (SRO)
papers.approach: Nanoindentation experiments combined with nano-mechanical testing and multi-scale crystal plasticity modeling to evaluate the influence of SRO on slip behavior and strain localization.
papers.findings: The presence of SRO increases hardness and creates higher heterogeneity in shear strain and reveals a greater density of geometrically necessary dislocations than in a randomized alloy structure.
papers.mechanism: SRO impedes dislocation slip by increasing the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation and motion, thus leading to more localized plasticity and a higher overall strength.

established: Severe lattice distortion and compositional complexity in high-entropy alloys lead to unusual deformation behavior compared to conventional metallic multilayers.
Interfaces, lattice misfit, and SRO play critical roles in governing dislocation nucleation, motion, and recoverability.
Dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is a dominant creep mechanism at lower stresses, whereas dynamic recrystallization and precipitation contribute at higher stresses.

approaches_tried.approach: Nanoindentation and microcompression experiments combined with TEM observations.
approaches_tried.outcome: Revealed a transition from planar slip to homogeneous plasticity and highlighted the role of lattice distortion and SRO in impeding dislocation glide.

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations for creep studies in HEAs/HESAs under variable stress, temperature, and lattice misfit conditions.
approaches_tried.outcome: Elucidated the dependence of creep life on controlled negative lattice misfit and showed how the steady-state creep parameters vary with stress/temperature.

approaches_tried.approach: Comparative nanoindentation simulations on bcc HEAs with and without SRO.
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that SRO can enhance hardness by modifying dislocation nucleation and recovery dynamics.

mechanisms: Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion.
Dynamic recrystallization and precipitate formation acting as barriers to dislocation motion.
Severe lattice distortion and SRO creating local energetic barriers that impede long-range dislocation glide.
Cooperative nucleation of dislocations across multiple slip systems in response to constrained multilayer interfaces.
disagreements: Some studies attribute creep behavior primarily to dislocation climb (especially at lower stresses), while others emphasize the cooperative role of dynamic recrystallization and precipitation (at higher stresses).
The relative importance of SRO in modulating dislocation nucleation versus dislocation mobility is still under debate.
open_questions: In nanoscale multilayer HEA systems, how do compositional complexity and interface quality jointly control the transition between dislocation-mediated glide, climb, and recovery?
What are the dominant deformation responses under sustained loading in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers?
How do variations in SRO and lattice misfit at the nanoscale influence the balance between strength and deformation tolerance in these systems?
opportunities: Conduct controlled comparisons between monolithic HEA films and nanoscale multilayer coatings with matched overall composition but differing interface/misorientation characteristics to isolate the impact of interfaces.
Systematically vary the degree of SRO (e.g., via thermal or mechanical treatments) in HEA multilayers to correlate local chemical ordering with changes in creep life and plastic deformation patterns.

Combine atomistic simulations and in situ mechanical testing at varying temperatures and stress levels to map the transition conditions where dislocation climb gives way to dynamic recrystallization or even amorphization events.
Explore multilayer designs that incorporate optimized negative lattice misfit across interfaces to enhance phase stability and resistance to progressive plastic deformation.

directions.direction: Tuning chemical short‐range order (SRO) in the multilayer interfaces via post-deposition thermal treatments.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the uncertainty introduced by compositional complexity and SRO effects. Supported by evidence that SRO modifies dislocation nucleation barriers (see PMC11032334::web::003, PMC11642976::web::000). Feasible by annealing experiments and in situ microscopy.

directions.direction: Engineering lattice misfit across FCC/BCC interfaces to achieve moderate negative misfit.
directions.assessment: Addresses interface stability and its control of dislocation motion, as shown in MD simulation studies (PMC12842692::web::023, PMC12842692::web::025). Feasible via deposition control and compositional adjustment.

directions.direction: Inducing controlled nano-precipitation/dynamic recrystallization at or near interfaces under sustained load.
directions.assessment: Targets progressive plastic deformation at high stresses by forming barriers to dislocation motion. Supported by creep studies in HEAs (PMC7512559::web::022, PMC7512559::web::000). Implementation may require precise thermal-mechanical cycling.

directions.direction: Enhancing interface coherency through optimized deposition to promote cooperative dislocation activity.
directions.assessment: Aims to reduce strain localization by smoothing the multilayer interfaces, facilitating cooperative activation of multiple slip systems. This direction is supported by dislocation observations in low roughness multilayers (PMC12964539::web::007).

directions.direction: Atomistic modelling and in situ mechanical testing to map dislocation dynamics and transitions between glide, climb and recovery.
directions.assessment: Focuses on fundamental understanding by correlating atomistic simulations with experimental creep, though it is more indirect. It is highly informative but may not yield direct actionable control over the design.
